summary: Creates a registry for IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) and assigns an initial set of object identities to metrics defined in the IETF. It also sets rules for adding future metrics, with IANA administering the registry. It is a best current practice, later replaced by RFC 6248.

eli5.summary: Every measurement of network speed and delay gets its own ID card in a central list. This memo starts that list and says how new measurements get added.

subtitle: Assigning unique identifiers to network performance metrics

tldr.problem: Network performance metrics (like one-way delay, packet loss, jitter) are defined in many RFCs but have no common way to be referenced in management systems. Each system uses its own names and codes.
tldr.mechanism: Creates a registry where IANA assigns unique object identifiers (from SNMP/MIB) to each metric. The initial registry covers 33 metrics from IPPM working group RFCs, grouped by topic. New metrics are registered via specification review.
tldr.outcome: Management systems can now refer to metrics unambiguously, making it possible to build cross-platform performance monitoring. IPPM metrics are upgraded to a well-known, reusable resource.

facts.value: 7 (connectivity, delay, loss, round-trip, patterns, jitter, periodic)

today: RFC 4148 is a Best Current Practice that was later replaced by RFC 6248, which updated the registry with additional metrics. The framework and concept remain valid, and the initial metrics are still in use.

sections.title: Why Metrics Need Identifiers
sections.content:
The IETF IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) working group has defined many ways to measure network behavior: one-way delay, packet loss, delay variation (jitter), and more. These metrics are described in standards RFCs, but when a management system—say, a router or a monitoring tool—wants to report a metric, it has no standard way to name it.

Without a registry, two systems measuring the same thing (e.g., 'the 95th-percentile round-trip delay on this path') might call it by different names or codes, making it impossible to share the results. This memo creates a registry of object identifiers, drawn from the SNMP/MIB system, so metrics can be referred to uniquely.
sections.eli5: Before this, calling a metric was like pointing: 'that measurement you do'. Now, each metric gets a number, like 'metric 7', so anyone can say 'I'm reporting metric 7' and everyone knows what they mean.

sections.title: The Registry Framework
sections.content:
The registry uses the ianaIppmMetrics subtree from the SNMP object identifier space. This is a part of the management information base (MIB) where IANA can assign unique names and numbers.

Each metric in the registry gets an OBJECT-IDENTITY: a machine-readable name (like ietfOneWayDelay) and a numeric identifier (like 6). The initial registry lists 33 metrics across seven categories: connectivity, one-way delay, packet loss, round-trip delay, loss patterns, delay variation, and periodic streams.
sections.eli5: Think of the registry as a phonebook: each metric has an official name ('One-Way Delay') and an official number ('6'). Anyone building a tool can look up the number and know exactly which measurement they're talking about.

sections.title: Registering New Metrics
sections.content:
When future RFCs define new metrics, they can ask IANA to register them in this same space. The registration process uses Specification Required: the metric must be described in a stable, published document, and the name must follow SNMP naming rules (start with the organization, no hyphens, camelCase). IANA assigns the next available number sequentially.

An important rule: once a metric is assigned a number, that number is permanent and cannot be reused, even if the metric is obsoleted. If a new version of a metric is needed, it gets a new name and a new number. This ensures long-term stability of management systems that depend on the numbers.
sections.eli5: If someone invents a new type of measurement, they write it down, send it to IANA, and IANA gives it the next number. The numbers never change, so a program written in 2005 can still read data from 2025.

sections.title: The Initial Metric Set
sections.content:
The registry starts with 33 metrics from existing IPPM RFCs:

Connectivity: bidirectional and unidirectional connectivity, instant and over a time interval. One-way delay: raw delay, plus percentile, median, and minimum variants. Packet loss: one-way loss, plus percentiles and averages. Round-trip delay: delay to a target and back, with variants like those for one-way delay. Loss patterns: distance between losses, period between losses, noticeable loss rate. Jitter (ipdv): variation in one-way delay, measured various ways (percentile, peak-to-peak). Periodic streams: delay measurement using regularly spaced probe packets.
sections.eli5: The list includes 'does the network work', 'how slow is it', 'how many packets drop', 'how jumpy is the speed', and a few dozen more. Each one is a specific, technical way of measuring something about the network.
